blocks.text: 1. IVF

blocks.alt: Vectors are grouped into clusters with centroids

blocks.text: IVF covers an alternative approach based on clustering vectors into partitions, offering a fundamentally different strategy for the same ANN goal.
It groups vectors into clusters first, then searches only the most relevant clusters.
2. A Graph Versus A Clustering Approach
HNSW connects vectors into a navigable graph; IVF instead groups vectors into clusters.
These are two fundamentally different strategies for narrowing the search space before comparing vectors directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Algorithm","Core structure"],"rows":[["HNSW","A navigable graph of connected vectors"],["IVF","Clusters of vectors grouped around centroids"]]}

blocks.text: 3. What IVF Stands For
IVF stands for Inverted File Index, a term borrowed from traditional search engines.
Each cluster acts like a bucket that lists which vectors belong to it.
4. Building Clusters With Centroids

blocks.alt: All vectors go through K-means clustering to produce centroids

blocks.text: A clustering algorithm groups similar vectors together and computes a representative centroid for each group.
Every stored vector gets assigned to its nearest centroid's cluster.
5. Searching Only Relevant Clusters

blocks.alt: A query finds the nearest centroids, then searches only those clusters

blocks.text: A query first compares against the small set of centroids, not every vector.
Only a handful of closest clusters ever get their actual vectors compared in detail.
6. The nprobe Parameter

blocks.alt: A low nprobe searches fewer clusters while a high nprobe searches more

blocks.text: The number of clusters searched, often called nprobe, is IVF's core tunable knob.
Searching more clusters improves recall at the cost of slower queries.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Setting nprobe to one searches only the single closest cluster, making queries very fast but risking missed neighbors that happen to live in a nearby cluster instead.

blocks.text: 7. The Edge Boundary Problem

blocks.alt: A vector near a cluster boundary might be missed

blocks.text: A true nearest neighbor can sometimes sit just across a cluster boundary from the query.
Searching only the query's own nearest cluster can miss that neighbor entirely.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A vector sitting extremely close to a cluster boundary can end up assigned to a neighboring cluster rather than the one a nearby query would naturally search first, which is exactly the edge boundary problem.

blocks.text: 8. IVF Versus HNSW

blocks.alt: IVF uses clustering while HNSW uses a graph

blocks.text: IVF typically uses less memory than a graph based index.
HNSW often achieves higher recall at a given speed, trading that memory advantage away.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Algorithm","Typical tradeoff"],"rows":[["IVF","Lower memory usage, tunable via nprobe"],["HNSW","Higher recall at a given speed, higher memory usage"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When IVF Is A Strong Choice

blocks.alt: A large dataset with moderate recall needs points toward IVF

blocks.text: Memory constrained environments with large collections favor IVF.
Maximum recall at any memory cost, by contrast, often favors HNSW.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates clustering vectors and searching only the closest clusters.

code.content:
import random

def euclidean_distance(v1, v2):
    return sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) ** 0.5

def assign_to_clusters(vectors, centroids):
    clusters = {i: [] for i in range(len(centroids))}
    for idx, v in enumerate(vectors):
        closest_centroid = min(range(len(centroids)), key=lambda c: euclidean_distance(v, centroids[c]))
        clusters[closest_centroid].append(idx)
    return clusters

def ivf_search(query, vectors, centroids, clusters, nprobe=2):
    centroid_distances = sorted(range(len(centroids)), key=lambda c: euclidean_distance(query, centroids[c]))
    closest_clusters = centroid_distances[:nprobe]
    candidates = []
    for cluster_id in closest_clusters:
        candidates.extend(clusters[cluster_id])
    candidates.sort(key=lambda i: euclidean_distance(query, vectors[i]))
    return candidates[:5]

vectors = [[random.random() for _ in range(8)] for _ in range(1000)]
centroids = [[random.random() for _ in range(8)] for _ in range(10)]

clusters = assign_to_clusters(vectors, centroids)
query = [random.random() for _ in range(8)]

results = ivf_search(query, vectors, centroids, clusters, nprobe=2)
total_checked = sum(len(clusters[c]) for c in sorted(range(len(centroids)), key=lambda c: euclidean_distance(query, centroids[c]))[:2])

print(f"Total vectors in collection: {len(vectors)}")
print(f"Vectors checked using nprobe=2: {total_checked}")
print(f"Top results: {results}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows IVF checking only a small fraction of the collection by comparing against centroids first, instead of scanning every stored vector directly.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Setting nprobe too low, missing true neighbors that fall near a cluster boundary.
Building clusters without enough centroids, leaving each cluster too large to search efficiently.
Assuming IVF and HNSW are interchangeable without weighing their different memory and recall tradeoffs.
Never re-clustering as the underlying data distribution shifts significantly over time.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: IVF groups vectors into clusters first, then searches only the most relevant clusters.
HNSW connects vectors into a graph; IVF instead groups vectors into clusters around centroids.
IVF stands for Inverted File Index, a term borrowed from traditional search engines.
A clustering algorithm computes a representative centroid for each group of similar vectors.
A query compares against centroids first, then only searches the closest clusters in detail.
The nprobe parameter controls how many clusters get searched, trading recall against speed.
A true nearest neighbor can sometimes sit just across a cluster boundary and get missed.
IVF typically uses less memory than a graph based index, while HNSW often achieves higher recall.
